claim: The reconstruction of ancient insect ectoparasitism is challenging, mostly because of the extreme scarcity of fossils with obvious ectoparasitic features such as sucking-piercing mouthparts and specialized attachment organs.
source: The reconstruction of ancient insect ectoparasitism is challenging, mostly because of the extreme scarcity of fossils with obvious ectoparasitic features such as sucking-piercing mouthparts and specialized attachment organs.
evidence: This is a statement about the challenges in paleontology based on established knowledge about fossil scarcity.

claim: Qiyia jurassica is a bizarre fly larva (Diptera) from the Jurassic of China.
source: Here we describe a bizarre fly larva (Diptera), Qiyia jurassica gen. et sp. nov., from the Jurassic of China
evidence: The manuscript describes the discovery and naming of this new species with supporting fossil specimens.

claim: Qiyia jurassica represents a stem group of the tabanomorph family Athericidae.
source: Here we describe a bizarre fly larva (Diptera), Qiyia jurassica gen. et sp. nov., from the Jurassic of China, that represents a stem group of the tabanomorph family Athericidae.
evidence: This phylogenetic placement is based on morphological analysis of the fossil specimens.

claim: Qiyia jurassica exhibits adaptations to an aquatic habitat.
source: Q. jurassica exhibits adaptations to an aquatic habitat.
evidence: The manuscript describes multiple morphological features consistent with aquatic life.

claim: Qiyia jurassica has a thoracic sucker with six radial ridges, which is unique in insects.
source: it preserves an unusual combination of features including a thoracic sucker with six radial ridges, unique in insects
evidence: The fossil specimens show this structure, and the manuscript states its uniqueness among insects.

claim: Qiyia jurassica has piercing-sucking mouthparts for fluid feeding.
source: it preserves an unusual combination of features including a thoracic sucker with six radial ridges, unique in insects, piercing-sucking mouthparts for fluid feeding
evidence: The mandible morphology visible in the fossils supports this interpretation.

claim: Qiyia jurassica has crocheted ventral prolegs with upward directed bristles for anchoring and movement while submerged.
source: crocheted ventral prolegs with upward directed bristles for anchoring and movement while submerged
evidence: These structures are visible in the fossil specimens and their function is inferred from morphology.

claim: Qiyia jurassica was an aquatic ectoparasitic insect.
source: We demonstrate that Q. jurassica was an aquatic ectoparasitic insect
evidence: This conclusion is based on multiple morphological features observed in the fossils.

claim: Qiyia jurassica probably fed on the blood of salamanders.
source: We demonstrate that Q. jurassica was an aquatic ectoparasitic insect, probably feeding on the blood of salamanders.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-occurrence with salamanders and morphological adaptations.

claim: The finding reveals an extreme morphological specialization of fly larvae.
source: The finding reveals an extreme morphological specialization of fly larvae
evidence: This is an interpretive statement based on the unique morphological features observed.

claim: The finding broadens our understanding of the diversity of ectoparasitism in Mesozoic insects.
source: broadens our understanding of the diversity of ectoparasitism in Mesozoic insects
evidence: This represents a new type of ectoparasitism not previously documented in the Mesozoic.

claim: The early evolution of insect ectoparasites and their associations with hosts are poorly known.
source: The early evolution of insect ectoparasites and their associations with hosts are poorly known (Labandeira, 2002; Wappler et al., 2004; Grimaldi and Engel, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Giant fleas have been widely accepted as definite terrestrial ectoparasitic insects on dinosaurs, pterosaurs, or mammals.
source: Although several Mesozoic insects were regarded as putative ectoparasites, only giant fleas have been widely accepted as definite terrestrial ectoparasitic insects on dinosaurs, pterosaurs, or mammals (Gao et al., 2012, 2013b; Huang et al., 2012, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Five well-preserved specimens of Qiyia jurassica were found in the Middle Jurassic Daohugou beds of China.
source: Here we report on an aquatic ectoparasitic insect based on five well-preserved specimens from the Middle Jurassic Daohugou beds of China.
evidence: The manuscript describes the specimens and their provenance.

claim: These fossils are extremely rare among the approximately 300,000 fossil insects in the collections of the Nanjing Institute of Geology and Palaeontology and Shandong Tianyu Museum of Nature.
source: These fossils are extremely rare among the approximately 300,000 fossil insects in the collections of the Nanjing Institute of Geology and Palaeontology and Shandong Tianyu Museum of Nature.
evidence: This provides context about the rarity of the specimens based on collection data.

claim: Qiyia jurassica belongs to Order Diptera Linnaeus, 1758.
source: Order Diptera Linnaeus, 1758
evidence: This is the formal taxonomic classification provided in the systematic paleontology section.

claim: Qiyia jurassica belongs to Family Athericidae Stuckenberg, 1973.
source: Family Athericidae Stuckenberg, 1973
evidence: This is the formal taxonomic classification provided in the systematic paleontology section.

claim: The name 'Qiyia' is from the Chinese 'qiyi' meaning bizarre.
source: Qiyia is from the Chinese 'qiyi' meaning bizarre
evidence: This is stated in the etymology section.

claim: The name 'jurassica' is a reference to the Jurassic age of the fossils.
source: jurassica is a reference to the Jurassic age of the fossils
evidence: This is stated in the etymology section.

claim: All specimens are preserved as carbonaceous impressions on the surface of grey tuffaceous siltstone.
source: All specimens are preserved as carbonaceous impressions on the surface of grey tuffaceous siltstone (Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the preservation mode of the fossils with citation support.

claim: The fossils are from the Middle Jurassic Daohugou beds (approximately 165 million years old) of Ningcheng County, Inner Mongolia, China.
source: From the Middle Jurassic Daohugou beds (approximately 165 million years old) of Ningcheng County, Inner Mongolia, China (Liu et al., 2006).
evidence: This provides the geological age and location with citation support.

claim: Qiyia jurassica has three thoracic segments fused, with a ventral sucker.
source: Three thoracic segments fused, with a ventral sucker
evidence: This is part of the diagnostic description and visible in the fossil specimens.

claim: Qiyia jurassica has two pairs of dorsal spines on abdominal segments 1–7.
source: two pairs of dorsal spines on abdominal segments 1–7
evidence: This is part of the diagnostic description and visible in the fossil specimens.

claim: Qiyia jurassica has abdominal segments 1–6 with paired ventral prolegs bearing upward directed bristles and apical crochets.
source: abdominal segments 1–6 with paired ventral prolegs bearing upward directed bristles and apical crochets
evidence: This is part of the diagnostic description and visible in the fossil specimens.

claim: Qiyia jurassica has an extended seventh proleg.
source: extended seventh proleg
evidence: This is part of the diagnostic description and visible in the fossil specimens.

claim: Qiyia jurassica has two pairs of anal papillae.
source: two pairs of anal papillae
evidence: This is part of the diagnostic description and visible in the fossil specimens.

claim: Qiyia jurassica has sclerotized terminal processes with stiff setae.
source: sclerotized terminal processes with stiff setae
evidence: This is part of the diagnostic description and visible in the fossil specimens.

claim: The body of Qiyia jurassica is elongate, 18–24 mm long.
source: Body elongate, 18–24 mm long (Table 1).
evidence: This measurement is based on the fossil specimens and presented in Table 1.

claim: The head of Qiyia jurassica is greatly reduced and partly retractile into thorax.
source: Head greatly reduced and partly retractile into thorax (Figure 1A,B)
evidence: This is observed in the fossil specimens shown in the figures.

claim: Antennae and eyes are not visible in Qiyia jurassica.
source: antennae and eyes not visible (Figure 1C)
evidence: This is an observation from the fossil specimens.

claim: Qiyia jurassica has a pair of sclerotized tentorial rods.
source: a pair of sclerotized tentorial rods (Figure 2B)
evidence: This structure is visible in the fossil specimens.

claim: The mandibles of Qiyia jurassica are approximately 0.6 mm long.
source: Mandibles approximately 0.6 mm long
evidence: This measurement is based on the fossil specimens.

claim: The mandibles of Qiyia jurassica are heavily sclerotized and sickle-shaped.
source: Mandibles approximately 0.6 mm long, heavily sclerotized, sickle-shaped
evidence: This morphology is observed in the fossil specimens.

claim: The mandibles of Qiyia jurassica are oriented to move parallel to each other in vertical plane.
source: oriented to move parallel to each other in vertical plane
evidence: This is inferred from the morphology and orientation of the mandibles in the fossils.

claim: The mandibles of Qiyia jurassica have an external groove on adoral surface extending whole length of mandible.
source: with external groove on adoral surface extending whole length of mandible (Figure 1E)
evidence: This feature is visible in the fossil specimens.

claim: The thoracic segment of Qiyia jurassica is swollen and slightly narrower than abdomen.
source: Thoracic segment swollen, slightly narrower than abdomen (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is observed in the fossil specimens.

claim: The sucker of Qiyia jurassica is retractile with a diameter about 2 mm.
source: Sucker retractile, diameter about 2 mm
evidence: This measurement and observation are based on the fossil specimens.

claim: The sucker is located ventrally on thoracic segment and consists of a circular suction disc with central opening about one quarter of disc diameter.
source: located ventrally on thoracic segment and consisting of a circular suction disc with central opening about one quarter of disc diameter
evidence: This morphology is observed in the fossil specimens.

claim: The peripheral area of the disc is thin and flexible.
source: peripheral area of disc thin and flexible (Figure 1D)
evidence: This is inferred from the preservation and appearance in the fossils.

claim: Six robust, sclerotized ridges are present on the sucker, radially arranged, covered by soft skin with small spines.
source: Six robust, sclerotized ridges on sucker, radially arranged, covered by soft skin with small spines (Figure 2D,E)
evidence: This structure is visible in the fossil specimens.

claim: The distal part of each ridge is thickened, probably with three processes embedded in musculature.
source: distal part of each ridge thickened, probably with three processes embedded in musculature (Figure 2E)
evidence: This is observed in the fossils with some inference about the embedded processes.

claim: Qiyia jurassica has three pairs of small spines with simple shafts on dorsolateral margins of thorax.
source: Three pairs of small spines with simple shafts on dorsolateral margins of thorax
evidence: This is observed in the fossil specimens.

claim: Qiyia jurassica has two pairs of spines on dorsolateral margins of abdominal segments 1–7.
source: two pairs on dorsolateral margins of abdominal segments 1–7
evidence: This is observed in the fossil specimens.

claim: Qiyia jurassica has one pair of spines on abdominal segment 8.
source: one pair on abdominal segment 8 (Figure 2A)
evidence: This is observed in the fossil specimens.

claim: The abdomen of Qiyia jurassica has eight distinct segments, covered by many short setae.
source: Abdomen with eight distinct segments, covered by many short setae.
evidence: This is observed in the fossil specimens.

claim: Each proleg of Qiyia jurassica is nearly half width of body with two rows of six crochet hooks apically.
source: each proleg nearly half width of body with two rows of six crochet hooks apically (Figure 1F)
evidence: This is observed in the fossil specimens.

claim: The seventh proleg is approximately three times longer than other prolegs with only three or four apical hooks.
source: seventh proleg approximately three times longer than other prolegs with only three or four apical hooks
evidence: This is observed in the fossil specimens.

claim: Abdominal segment 8 has two pairs of slender, tapering anal papillae: first pair long, approximately quarter body length; second pair half the length of the first pair.
source: abdominal segment 8 with two pairs of slender, tapering anal papillae: first pair long, approximately quarter body length; second pair half the length of the first pair (Figure 1A,B)
evidence: This is observed and measured in the fossil specimens.

claim: Qiyia jurassica has one pair of unsegmented, sclerotized terminal processes fringed with stiff setae, approximately one-tenth body length.
source: one pair of unsegmented, sclerotized terminal processes fringed with stiff setae, approximately one-tenth body length
evidence: This is observed in the fossil specimens.

claim: Each terminal process has about 10 spiracles.
source: each process with about 10 spiracles (Figure 1G, Figure 2C)
evidence: This is observed in the fossil specimens.

claim: Three specimens are laterally compressed (STMN65-1, STMN65-2, NIGP156984) and two are dorsoventrally compressed (NIGP156982, NIGP156983).
source: Three specimens are laterally compressed (STMN65-1, STMN65-2, NIGP156984) and two are dorsoventrally compressed (NIGP156982, NIGP156983)
evidence: This describes the preservation mode of the different specimens.

claim: The different compression modes provide side and top views of the detailed morphology of the larva.
source: Three specimens are laterally compressed (STMN65-1, STMN65-2, NIGP156984) and two are dorsoventrally compressed (NIGP156982, NIGP156983), thereby providing side and top views of the detailed morphology of the larva.
evidence: This is an inference about how the different preservation modes contribute to understanding morphology.

claim: Q. jurassica is attributed to the Tabanomorpha by the reduced and retractable head and sickle-shaped mandibles shifted into a vertical plane.
source: Q. jurassica is attributed to the Tabanomorpha by the reduced and retractable head and sickle-shaped mandibles shifted into a vertical plane (Yeates, 2002; Zloty et al., 2005).
evidence: This phylogenetic attribution is based on morphological characters with citation support.

claim: Q. jurassica possesses mandibles with external grooves, which is a noticeably plesiomorphic feature.
source: It possesses two noticeably plesiomorphic features: mandibles with external grooves (Zloty et al., 2005)
evidence: This character state is identified as primitive with citation support.

claim: Q. jurassica possesses well-developed anal papillae, which is a noticeably plesiomorphic feature.
source: It possesses two noticeably plesiomorphic features: mandibles with external grooves (Zloty et al., 2005) and well-developed anal papillae (Wichard et al., 1999)
evidence: This character state is identified as primitive with citation support.

claim: Q. jurassica shares paired prolegs with crochet hooks as a potential synapomorphy with extant athericid larvae.
source: while sharing two potential synapomorphies with extant athericid larvae: paired prolegs with crochet hooks (Yeates, 2002; Kerr, 2010)
evidence: This shared derived character is identified with citation support.

claim: Q. jurassica shares long terminal processes fringed with setae as a potential synapomorphy with extant athericid larvae.
source: while sharing two potential synapomorphies with extant athericid larvae: paired prolegs with crochet hooks (Yeates, 2002; Kerr, 2010) and long terminal processes fringed with setae (Dobson, 2013)
evidence: This shared derived character is identified with citation support.

claim: The combination of primitive and derived features demonstrates that Q. jurassica is a stem lineage representative of the Athericidae.
source: This combination of primitive and derived features demonstrates that Q. jurassica is a stem lineage representative of the Athericidae (water snipe flies), a family sister to the more familiar horse flies (Tabanidae).
evidence: This phylogenetic interpretation is based on character analysis.

claim: Athericidae is a family sister to the Tabanidae (horse flies).
source: This combination of primitive and derived features demonstrates that Q. jurassica is a stem lineage representative of the Athericidae (water snipe flies), a family sister to the more familiar horse flies (Tabanidae).
evidence: This phylogenetic relationship is stated based on established knowledge.

claim: The earliest known Athericidae and Tabanidae (all represented by preserved adults) are from the Early Cretaceous of southern England.
source: The earliest known Athericidae and Tabanidae (all represented by preserved adults) are from the Early Cretaceous of southern England (Mostovski et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The new fossils are the earliest record of athericid flies and extend the lineage back to the Middle Jurassic.
source: Our new fossils are the earliest record of athericid flies and extend the lineage back to the Middle Jurassic
evidence: This is based on the age of the Daohugou beds and comparison with previous records.

claim: The Middle Jurassic age is consistent with predicted divergence times based on molecular studies (estimated at the Early or Middle Jurassic).
source: an age which is consistent with predicted divergence times based on molecular studies (estimated at the Early or Middle Jurassic) (Wiegmann et al., 2011)
evidence: This comparison is supported by citation to molecular phylogenetic studies.

claim: Extant Athericidae are aquatic predators in fast-flowing water.
source: much like extant Athericidae which are today aquatic predators in fast-flowing water (as adults some athericids feed on mammalian or amphibian blood) (Mostovski et al., 2003; Nagatomi and Stuckenberg, 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on extant species.

claim: As adults some athericids feed on mammalian or amphibian blood.
source: much like extant Athericidae which are today aquatic predators in fast-flowing water (as adults some athericids feed on mammalian or amphibian blood) (Mostovski et al., 2003; Nagatomi and Stuckenberg, 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on extant species.

claim: The paired sclerotized terminal processes are morphologically comparable to the modifications of beetle urogomphi in the aquatic larvae of some families such as Dytiscidae.
source: The paired sclerotized terminal processes are morphologically comparable to the modifications of beetle urogomphi in the aquatic larvae of some families such as Dytiscidae (Wichard et al., 1999).
evidence: This comparison is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The terminal processes of Q. jurassica were used for breathing air.
source: About 10 spiracles are present on each process of Q. jurassica (Figure 1G, Figure 2C), confirming that they were used for breathing air
evidence: This functional interpretation is based on the presence of spiracles.

claim: The terminal processes are functionally similar to the unsclerotized ones of extant athericid larvae.
source: About 10 spiracles are present on each process of Q. jurassica (Figure 1G, Figure 2C), confirming that they were used for breathing air, functionally similar to the unsclerotized ones of extant athericid larvae (Nagatomi and Stuckenberg, 2004).
evidence: This functional comparison is supported by citation.

claim: Anal papillae are useful for extracting dissolved oxygen from water in aquatic flies.
source: Q. jurassica also possesses two pairs of anal papillae which are useful for extracting dissolved oxygen from water in aquatic flies and also play an important part in salt absorption to maintain ionic concentrations in the body fluids (Wichard et al., 1999).
evidence: This functional interpretation is supported by citation.

claim: Anal papillae play an important part in salt absorption to maintain ionic concentrations in the body fluids.
source: Q. jurassica also possesses two pairs of anal papillae which are useful for extracting dissolved oxygen from water in aquatic flies and also play an important part in salt absorption to maintain ionic concentrations in the body fluids (Wichard et al., 1999).
evidence: This functional interpretation is supported by citation.

claim: Anal papillae are common in nematoceran larvae and in some lower brachyceran larvae.
source: These organs are common in nematoceran larvae and in some lower brachyceran larvae, but are reduced in extant tabanomorphan larvae (Wichard et al., 1999; Dobson, 2013).
evidence: This comparative statement is supported by citations.

claim: Anal papillae are reduced in extant tabanomorphan larvae.
source: These organs are common in nematoceran larvae and in some lower brachyceran larvae, but are reduced in extant tabanomorphan larvae (Wichard et al., 1999; Dobson, 2013).
evidence: This comparative statement is supported by citations.

claim: In the case of the fossil larva, the development of anal papillae implies a plesiomorphic condition.
source: In the case of the fossil larva, their development implies a plesiomorphic condition.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison with extant taxa.

claim: The ridged thoracic sucker is a unique evolutionary adaptation among holometabolous insects.
source: The most notable structure of these newly discovered fossils is the ridged thoracic sucker which is a unique evolutionary adaptation among holometabolous insects.
evidence: This uniqueness is stated based on comparison with known holometabolous insects.

claim: The six radial ridges are considered to be highly modified thoracic legs.
source: The round sucker has six radial ridges which are considered to be highly modified thoracic legs (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the homology of these structures.

claim: The six robust, sclerotized ridges could increase both the suction area and surface friction, thus providing more adhesion and increasing lateral stability whilst reducing slippage.
source: These six robust, sclerotized ridges could increase both the suction area and surface friction, thus providing more adhesion and increasing lateral stability whilst reducing slippage, like the radial grooves in modern octopus suckers (Kier and Smith, 2002) and supporting ribs in man-made suction cups (Monkman et al., 2007).
evidence: This functional interpretation is supported by analogies with citations.

claim: The dense vestiture of small spines may be used for better anchoring on the corrugated skin of a salamander.
source: The dense vestiture of small spines may be used for better anchoring on the corrugated skin of a salamander, like the sucker-ring teeth and knobs on squid suckers (e.g., Miserez et al., 2009).
evidence: This functional interpretation is supported by analogy with citation.

claim: Among insect larvae, only extant blepharicerids (Diptera) have six well-developed suckers, but these are small and without ridges on the abdominal sternites.
source: To our knowledge, among insect larvae, only extant blepharicerids (Diptera) have six well-developed suckers, but these are small and without ridges on the abdominal sternites.
evidence: This comparative statement is based on knowledge of insect larvae.

claim: Blepharicerid larvae graze on periphyton on rocks and use the suckers to adhere to the substrate in fast-flowing streams.
source: As blepharicerid larvae graze on periphyton on rocks, they use the suckers to adhere to the substrate in fast-flowing streams (Frutiger, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The excellent preservation of the new fossils suggests that Q. jurassica did not travel long distances.
source: However, the excellent preservation of our new fossils suggests that Q. jurassica did not travel long distances
evidence: This is inferred from the preservation quality.

claim: Unlike crown group Athericidae, Q. jurassica most probably lived in still water near to or in the Daohugou palaeolake.
source: and, unlike crown group Athericidae, most probably lived in still water near to or in the Daohugou palaeolake, a low-energy preservation environment (Wang et al., 2013)
evidence: This is inferred from the preservation environment with citation support.

claim: The Daohugou palaeolake was a low-energy preservation environment.
source: and, unlike crown group Athericidae, most probably lived in still water near to or in the Daohugou palaeolake, a low-energy preservation environment (Wang et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: When anchored to the substrate, the thoracic sucker probably restricted the movement of the small, short head.
source: The thoracic sucker on Q. jurassica is strongly cephalad on the body so, when anchored to the substrate, it probably restricted the movement of the small, short head (Figure 1D, Figure 2E)
evidence: This is inferred from the position and morphology of the sucker.

claim: The restricted head movement is clearly suitable for piercing and sucking.
source: The thoracic sucker on Q. jurassica is strongly cephalad on the body so, when anchored to the substrate, it probably restricted the movement of the small, short head (Figure 1D, Figure 2E), a condition that is clearly suitable for piercing and sucking (Figure 3).
evidence: This functional interpretation is based on morphology.

claim: Suckers are widespread in aquatic ectoparasites such as leeches, fish lice, and lampreys.
source: Suckers are widespread in aquatic ectoparasites such as leeches, fish lice, and lampreys (Kearn, 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Aquatic ectoparasites require more suction power to avoid becoming dislodged.
source: Suckers are widespread in aquatic ectoparasites such as leeches, fish lice, and lampreys (Kearn, 2004) which require more suction power to avoid becoming dislodged
evidence: This is supported by citation and general knowledge.

claim: Other aquatic ectoparasites without attachment organs embed themselves in skin or muscle, such as cyclopoid copepods (anchor worms).
source: other aquatic ectoparasites without attachment organs embed themselves in skin or muscle, such as cyclopoid copepods (anchor worms) (Kearn, 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The stiff, upward directed bristles and apical hooks on the prolegs are specialized attachment structures.
source: In addition to the sucker, the stiff, upward directed bristles and apical hooks on the prolegs (Figure 1F) are also specialized attachment structures.
evidence: This functional interpretation is based on morphology.

claim: These morphological adaptations provide compelling evidence that Q. jurassica adhered to a host as an ectoparasite.
source: These morphological adaptations provide compelling evidence that Q. jurassica adhered to a host as an ectoparasite
evidence: This conclusion is based on multiple morphological features.

claim: The morphological adaptations provide further specialization for a dense, watery habitat.
source: These morphological adaptations provide compelling evidence that Q. jurassica adhered to a host as an ectoparasite, providing further specialization for a dense, watery habitat.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of features.

claim: Bloodsucking is considered to have evolved independently at least 12 times in true flies.
source: Bloodsucking is considered to have evolved independently at least 12 times in true flies (Lukashevich and Mostovski, 2003; Wiegmann et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Bloodsucking started with free-living scavengers or predators which subsequently became opportunistic feeders on vertebrates.
source: It started with free-living scavengers or predators which subsequently became opportunistic feeders on vertebrates, such as the notorious Congo floor maggot (Auchmeromyia) that consumes the blood of sleeping humans (Lehane, 2005).
evidence: This evolutionary scenario is supported by citation.

claim: The Congo floor maggot (Auchmeromyia) consumes the blood of sleeping humans.
source: such as the notorious Congo floor maggot (Auchmeromyia) that consumes the blood of sleeping humans (Lehane, 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Bloodsuckers are present as adults in three families of extant Tabanomorpha.
source: Bloodsuckers are present as adults in three families of extant Tabanomorpha (Nagatomi and Stuckenberg, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Hitherto known larval Tabanomorpha are mainly predators.
source: Although hitherto known larval Tabanomorpha are mainly predators
evidence: This is based on knowledge of extant species.

claim: Some larvae suck the body fluids of vertebrates such as anurans.
source: Although hitherto known larval Tabanomorpha are mainly predators, some larvae suck the body fluids of vertebrates such as anurans (Jackman et al., 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Predatory fly larvae commonly have morphological and physiological adaptations (such as efficient protein-digesting enzymes and salivary glands), facilitating the switch to bloodsucking.
source: Predatory fly larvae commonly have morphological and physiological adaptations (such as efficient protein-digesting enzymes and salivary glands), facilitating the switch to bloodsucking (Balashov, 1984; Lehane, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The sickle-shaped mandibles with external grooves form a channel when the left and right mandibles are occluded.
source: Q. jurassica has a pair of sickle-shaped mandibles with external grooves (Figure 1E), which is a groundplan character of Tabanomorpha (Wichard et al., 1999; Yeates, 2002), forming a channel when the left and right mandibles are occluded (Zloty et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The mandibular channel is used for sucking blood or other body fluids.
source: forming a channel when the left and right mandibles are occluded (Zloty et al., 2005) and used for sucking blood or other body fluids (Marshall, 1981)
evidence: This functional interpretation is supported by citation.

claim: In the Daohugou deposits fish are completely absent.
source: In the Daohugou deposits fish are completely absent but salamanders are extremely abundant (several thousand specimens recovered to date) (Liu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is based on the fossil record with citation support.

claim: Salamanders are extremely abundant in the Daohugou deposits (several thousand specimens recovered to date).
source: In the Daohugou deposits fish are completely absent but salamanders are extremely abundant (several thousand specimens recovered to date) (Liu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is based on the fossil record with citation support.

claim: The most common salamanders at Daohugou are Chunerpeton tianyiensis and Jeholotriton paradoxus.
source: The most common salamanders at Daohugou, Chunerpeton tianyiensis and Jeholotriton paradoxus, have body lengths of 500 mm and 150 mm, respectively (Wang and Rose, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Chunerpeton tianyiensis has a body length of 500 mm.
source: The most common salamanders at Daohugou, Chunerpeton tianyiensis and Jeholotriton paradoxus, have body lengths of 500 mm and 150 mm, respectively (Wang and Rose, 2005).
evidence: This measurement is supported by citation.

claim: Jeholotriton paradoxus has a body length of 150 mm.
source: The most common salamanders at Daohugou, Chunerpeton tianyiensis and Jeholotriton paradoxus, have body lengths of 500 mm and 150 mm, respectively (Wang and Rose, 2005).
evidence: This measurement is supported by citation.

claim: Both Chunerpeton tianyiensis and Jeholotriton paradoxus display neotenic features and are fully aquatic in all stages of their life cycle.
source: Both species display neotenic features and are fully aquatic in all stages of their life cycle (Gao et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Salamander skin is glabrous and thin, and could easily have been penetrated by the mandibles of a larva such as Q. jurassica.
source: Salamander skin is glabrous and thin, and could easily have been penetrated by the mandibles of a larva such as Q. jurassica.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of salamander anatomy and inference about the fossil.

claim: The Daohugou salamanders match Q. jurassica well in size as well as co-occurrence, suggesting a possible parasite-host relationship.
source: The Daohugou salamanders match Q. jurassica well in size as well as co-occurrence, suggesting a possible parasite-host relationship.
evidence: This is inferred from the fossil record and size compatibility.

claim: Some extant fly larvae parasitize anurans by burrowing into the skin, including Calliphoridae, Sarcophagidae, and Chloropidae.

claim: Previous definite Mesozoic ectoparasitic insect records were confined to the terrestrial giant fleas from the Middle Jurassic and Early Cretaceous epochs.
source: Despite a great taxonomic diversity of extant ectoparasitic insects (Marshall, 1981), previous definite Mesozoic records were confined to the terrestrial giant fleas from the Middle Jurassic and Early Cretaceous epochs (Gao et al., 2012, 2013b; Huang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.
